articles.text: England never had a greater white elephant on her hands than Riel is proving to be. Canada has convicted him but dare not hang him and England is afraid to decide the question. Whether Riel is hung or allowed to go free a large faction of Canadians will become disaffected.
articles.summary: Editorial note on the dilemma Louis Riel's conviction poses for Canada and England.

articles.text: A late report issued by the Bureau of Statistics, at Washington, is strongly in favor of a National cattle trail and declares that it is a necessity. Northern ranchmen, who have had their ranges damaged or ruined by grasshoppers, drought or prairie fires hardly think this.
articles.summary: Northern ranchmen are said to disagree with a Bureau of Statistics report favoring a National cattle trail.

articles.text: The labor troubles in Washington Territory and other places in the west have assumed serious proportions for the Chinese. It seems that in spite of the law restricting the immigration of Chinamen, large numbers have been landed in British America and thence come overland into the United States. Washington Territory especially is already overcrowded with whites and this influx of Chinese is added to the already large number of idle whites. The whole has culminated in a determination to rid the country of Chinamen and the initiative has already been taken by several trades-unions. Every effort will be made to drive them back to the land of birds' nest soup and rat porridge.
articles.summary: Editorial on anti-Chinese labor agitation in Washington Territory, written in the hostile language of the period.

articles.text: With all the attention to business details, which characterizes the cattle business, it seems strange that cattlemen should depend almost entirely on commission men to conduct their sales. Of course it is the simplest and easiest way to dispose of cattle but we doubt if it is the most profitable. The commission man sells at whatever price he chooses, deducts his commission and expenses and gives the balance to the cattleman. It is astonishing that the commission men are as honest as the lack of serious complaint shows them to be. It would be a very simple thing to have an understanding between the buyer and the commission man and make the seller lose the "cahoots." A remedy for this is hard to find but it seems strange that some move is not made toward limiting the absolute power of the commission men in making sales. We confess that these remarks arise from a well-founded ill-will the editor has for commission men in another line of business. Lately, however, we have seen two cattlemen who are seriously dissatisfied with the present way of making sales. It is a matter that should be considered by stock organizations.
articles.summary: Editorial urging stock organizations to curb the power of commission men who sell cattlemen's stock.

articles.text: Never, since this country was first settled, have there been such extensive and destructive prairie fires as have raged within the last three weeks. The general limits of the fires, as nearly as can be learned, are Jamestown on the east, between Mingusville and Glendive on the west, the Killdeer Mts., to the bend in the Little Missouri and north of the Yellowstone on the north and as far as Cave Hills on the south. Of course we do not mean that the whole country within these limits is burned clean, but that half of it is a blackened waste, is a moderate estimate. The damage done to the agriculturalists of Dakota, must be over $100,000, in the loss of grain, houses, stock, implements etc. To the cattle interests also, the danger is menacing. The Bad Lands form a pretty effectual fire-break on account of the numerous wash-outs and bare places, but many coulies and ravines leading in from the prairies both east and west have acted as regular flues to lead the fire into the Bad Lands and in some cases, clear to the river. Tongues of fire have fairly riddled the whole country. This makes the question of finding sufficient range for cattle, a serious one. It is a matter of doubt even now, if there is enough unburned range to pasture the cattle now in the Bad Lands and as we write these words the air is full of smoke from the still burning fires. There are still some ranges untouched, but they are liable to be pretty well crowded this winter by cattle from the burned ranges. We have heard that several new outfits intended driving into the Bad Lands this winter, but the fires must have caused a change of programme. No experienced cattleman would think of taking the risk involved by such a move.
articles.summary: The paper reports the most destructive prairie fires since settlement, burning across western Dakota and into the Bad Lands over the past three weeks and threatening winter range.

articles.summary: T. R. Selmes of Mandan attended the Cantonment sales Monday as attorney for the estate.

articles.text: Abe. Goodkind of Bismarck, was here this morning, making the buttes and coulies fairly ring with praises of the "Far West" and "Our Pet" cigars.
articles.summary: Abe Goodkind of Bismarck was in Medora promoting "Far West" and "Our Pet" cigars.

articles.text: Judge Francis and clerk of the Supreme court Haight arrived Sunday night and started Tuesday for Deadwood, for the session of court there. While here they were guests of the Marquis.
articles.summary: Judge Francis and Supreme Court clerk Haight stayed as guests of the Marquis before leaving for court at Deadwood.

articles.text: A deer was killed by the cars at Sully Springs yesterday, being the only case of the kind on record, as far as our knowledge goes. The pilot of the engine was also badly demoralized.
articles.summary: A deer was killed by a train at Sully Springs.

articles.text: One of Osborne Bros. Polled Angus heifers was killed by a train Monday. Such a loss is more serious than usual, as the railroad will probably pay no more for it than they would an ordinary animal.
articles.summary: A Polled Angus heifer of Osborne Bros. was killed by a train.

articles.text: The market report of this issue presents but little of interest to our readers. Northern wintered Texans are quoted the same as last week, while the lowest price on northern range cattle has raised and the highest price lowered, twenty-five cents. The combined receipts of cattle at Chicago, New York, Kansas City and St. Louis, were 70,840, of which Chicago received about 38,000. The cattle averaged poorer in quality than the week before and the reason the price kept up was that buyers were present from New York, Boston and Baltimore, who bought freely. Dressed-beef operators also furnished competition.
articles.summary: Comment on the week's cattle market and receipts.

articles.text: The Texas Live Stock Journal lays the great loss in cattle there last winter to the practice of allowing bulls to run with the herd the year round.
articles.summary: Texas losses last winter blamed on letting bulls run with herds year round.

articles.text: The Maltese cross, Quarter circle diamond and L C outfits will gather all their bulls this fall and feed them near the Big Plateau. Sufficient hay has already been provided.
articles.summary: The Maltese Cross, Quarter Circle Diamond and LC outfits will gather their bulls this fall and feed them near the Big Plateau.

articles.text: It seems that the branding of all calves by the Bad Lands Co., as mentioned in our last issue, was not the first time it has been done in the Bad Lands. We can however, repeat our commendation of the act, as it is liable to save many dollars to neighboring outfits and is an act that will certainly be appreciated by any one. We hope to see it universally practised hereafter.
articles.summary: The paper again commends the Bad Lands Co. for branding all calves, though it was not the first outfit to do so.

articles.text: As we have before stated, there are a number of minor points about the cattle business in the Bad Lands, which are still in their experimental stage. The one of most importance is the value of keeping herds off the river bottoms in the winter. Several outfits have made preparations to keep all their cattle back from the river, and thoroughly test the matter. On account of the fires, however, it will be impossible to arrive at decisive results this winter, as the feed is decreased by at least one-third.
articles.summary: Several outfits plan to keep cattle off the river bottoms this winter, though the fires have cut feed by a third.

articles.text: It is hard to believe that the bottom is so knocked out of the Chicago market that the Bad Lands cattle Co's cattle, only brought $3.85 and $4. We learn however, that they did not average 1200 lbs. which accounts in a measure for the low price. Their being in such fine condition at the start was deceptive. Perhaps Will. Dantz' experience may also explain the low price. His cattle refused food and water during the most or all of the trip to Chicago. After leaving St. Paul, a fog from Lake Michigan was encountered that made the floors of the cars so slippery as to keep the cattle constantly off their feet. Sometimes over half a car load would be down at once. Of course, when they were unloaded they looked gaunt and in poor condition, no matter how they looked when loaded. Such a series of mishaps would be fatal to a high price for any kind of stock.
articles.summary: Bad Lands Cattle Co. cattle brought only $3.85 and $4 in Chicago; Will Dantz's shipment suffered on the trip.

articles.text: Bill Jones tackled a broncho when the round-up started, Tuesday morning, that could have given points to Mark Twain's prize bucker. Bill says that he had Joe McCoul's coat on when he started up and Joe yelled to him to throw it down if he didn't get back in time to join the round-up. When he came down he spoiled a fine brand-new stump with the back of his head. That is, it posessed no further utility as a stump. As kindling it would have topped the market. It seemed "sorter" like tempting Providence for Bill to mount that mild-mannered looking brute again but he did and Bill says he couldn't hear the little birds sing until some time after on the way down. This time he lit in some buffalo berry bushes and the bronch., going in to see if he was hurt walked all over him, repeated and did it again. Bill led the brute into town, got spliced up, and yesterday morning was seen rounding the slaughter-house on the way to the round-up, holding on to leather with a life-preserver, blanket roll on the horn, and hobbled stirrups, while Uberman and Bemis were herding him out of town.
articles.summary: Bill Jones was twice thrown by a bucking broncho as the round-up started, then rode out again the next day.

articles.headline: Dehorning Cattle.
articles.text: I hereby give you a bit of my experience in the way of sawing off horns. Mr. Haaff's last letter seemed to lay the matter down so simply that a neighbor offered to furnish the subject if I would wield the saw. Being desirous of seeing the experiment tried, I readily consented. The animal was a two-year-old shorthorn bull that had shown strong symptoms of viciousness, having backed the owner out of pasture two or three times. Our first attempt proved futile, failing to secure the brute properly. The head was tied around as Mr. Haaff directs, but the stanchions gave way, and out went Mr. Bull with a horn half off. We were obliged to abandon the job till next morning, when a suitable stanchion was fixed. This time the Hon. Gentleman left the stable a hornless muley, not having lost any more blood than would naturally flow from a cut on your finger. Not a groan did he give, but threw himself down, and there he lay till the horns dropped in the manger before him. About an hour afterward we made him a visit in the pasture, found him feeding as quietly as though nothing had happened, suffering no perceptible inconveniende, only that he could not gore us. There are several others in this vicinity who will soon share the same fate. Some very humane people denounce us as cruel and unfeeling, and are somewhat inclined to complain of us. But let them once get horned by a mad bull and I'll venture they will be willing to see the brute sawed in two in the middle. I now believe "dehorning" perfectly harmless, as well as a benefit to the herd. I intend to denude my cattle of horns at an early date. The operation was performed four weeks ago; bull all right yet.—[I. E. S., in Western Rural.
articles.summary: Clipped letter from the Western Rural describing a successful dehorning of a bull.

articles.headline: The Cattle Trail.
articles.text:
A few facts may be of some interest to your many readers if you will allow me to give them through the columns of your valuable paper. I have taken a trip this spring by the way of Abilene, Colorado, thence north in the Panhandle and back home again on a round trip. I noticed a great improvement in cattle; all seem to be trying to improve their stock, and to economize in every way to meet hard times. I find no improvement in the way of handling cattle. We see everything moved on the same jump. Here we go boys fifteen or twenty miles to a round-up, we ride at the rate of seven miles an hour, and often more. We cut our cattle and go back almost the same speed, reach camp with horses often ridden down, and I often noticed blood dripping from their sides and shoulders. The cattle are all so foot-sore, lame and driven so it will take a month to get over it. We often see yearlings that are a little hard to drive, roped, beaten, spurred, their eyes crammed full of sand, and very often killed with abuse. I cannot believe that owners of stock know altogether just how rough stock are handled. If they did, surely they would realize the damage done to them by the utter recklessness of every move in the handling of range cattle.

We notice the way of grazing herds. Yes, we see two or three hands down off their horses talking together, letting the cattle scatter over territory sufficient for three times the size of the herd, then they get on their horses, round them in on the jump, which is an injury to both horse and cow to some extent. Also when they drive on to the bed ground the movement is still too rapid, crowding them up and causing them to step on one another's feet. It accounts for 75 per cent. of the trail cattle being lame. There are other causes for the poor condition of driving cattle that could be prevented if the trail bosses would take more interest, stay about the herd and see what is going on, instead of being in camp so much of the time. There is as much in a boss knowing how to handle men as there is in knowing how to handle cattle. A man not knowing how to handle men, especially without showing partiality, is not a fit subject to be intrusted with the management of a trail herd. I claim to know of what I speak, having been on the trail almost yearly since 1871, and I am a man who ought to learn something in that time.—[Trail Driver in Texas Live Stock Journal.
articles.summary: Clipped letter from a Texas trail driver criticizing rough handling of range and trail cattle.

articles.summary: Local puff for the "Far West" cigar at Roberts & Co.

articles.summary: The Refrigerator Car Co. moved its general offices from St. Paul to Medora.

articles.text: J. W. Buster superintended the delivery of five hundred Hashknife cattle to the Co. this morning averaging 1066.
articles.summary: J. W. Buster delivered 500 Hashknife cattle averaging 1066 lbs to the Co.

articles.summary: Local puff for Roberts & Co.'s cigars.

articles.text: We are indebted to Mr. John Carr of Delavan, Ill., for late papers from his home. He returned home from his visit to Dick, with a very much and favorably changed idea of Dakota.
articles.summary: John Carr of Delavan, Ill., sent papers after returning home from a visit to Dick with a better opinion of Dakota.

articles.text: Sheriff Harmon has made many friends in Medora and if it laid with Billings county to give him a life lease on the office of sheriff in Morton county he would easily get it.
articles.summary: Sheriff Harmon of Morton county is popular in Medora.

articles.text: Geo. Porter left last week for Chicago and the east, on his annual purchasing tour for the Co's. general store. Messrs. Keeler and Grymes will hold down the store during his absence.
articles.summary: Geo. Porter left on his annual buying trip east for the company's general store.

articles.text: P. S. Bemis, of New York, lately of Ransom county, Dakota, came to Medora last Saturday and has joined the round-up. He intends getting a practical insight into the cattle business and may go into it.
articles.summary: P. S. Bemis of New York arrived and joined the round-up to learn the cattle business.

articles.text: At his recent trial in Miles City, Wm. Roberts was found guilty of stealing six horses at the Hashknife camp last winter. We hear that he has been sentenced to sixteen years in the penitentiary.
articles.summary: Wm. Roberts was convicted at Miles City of stealing six horses from the Hashknife camp.

articles.text: The round-up started from Medora Tuesday morning and is now at Wadsworths and will camp four miles below him tonight. The smoke bothers the boys greatly and it is feared that some of the cattle will be missed and that there will be a consequent increase of mavericks found in the spring.
articles.summary: The fall round-up left Medora Tuesday and is working down river past Wadsworth's in heavy smoke.

articles.text: Supt. Green was in town Saturday looking over the ground preparatory to building new stock yards here. No particulars have as yet been learned but on account of the difficulty of finding feed both at Dickinson and Mingusville it is probable that large ones will be built immediately.
articles.summary: Supt. Green examined ground for new stock yards at Medora.

articles.text: Postmaster Harbison, G. H. Zirngebel and Geo. E. Scales, of Belfield, attended the sale here Monday. The latter chartered a flat-car or something and brought along the prize potato of the season. It was raised near Belfield and except in size is said to be a fair sample of his crop. The West Missouri country ought to come to the front with such a vegetable to advertise it.
articles.summary: Belfield men attended Monday's sale; Geo. E. Scales brought a prize potato.

articles.text: Julius LeMoyne of Washington, Penn., and president of the LeMoyne cattle Co., arrived last Saturday evening from his home. It has been decided to keep the LC herd on its present range for this winter at least. Mr. LeMoyne thinks of starting a blooded herd here, for the purpose of raising range bulls, an enterprise we have hitherto advocated as offering greater profits than any other branch of the cattle business. Mr. LeMoyne is president of the Washington county breeder's association, in Pennsylvania and possesses great facilities for starting such a herd.
articles.summary: Julius LeMoyne arrived; the LC herd will winter on its present range and he may start a blooded herd to raise range bulls.

articles.text: Jos. W. Nimmo, Jr. ex-chief of the Bureau of Statistics and editor of "Range and Ranch Cattle Area of the United States," besides many other works was here Tuesday and yesterday and made us a very pleasant call. He is looking up facts soon to appear in a popular work on cattle raising. Mr. Nimmo goes east tomorrow morning but will return in a week and make his next stop west, at Miles city.
articles.summary: Joseph Nimmo Jr., former chief of the Bureau of Statistics, visited Medora and the Cow Boy office gathering facts on cattle raising.

articles.text: There is probably not a more successful mercantile institution on the line of the road than the Boston Clothing, Boot and Shoe store, in its various branches. Two causes have contributed to this success: an abundant use of printers ink to attract and hold custom and an honest and well-carried-out intention of giving value for value received. The first fact is illustrated by the large ad., appearing in this issue of the Cow Boy, and the second can easily be proven by a visit to the Medora branch of this institution, presided over by T. W. Gordon.
articles.summary: Praise for the Boston Clothing, Boot and Shoe store and its Medora branch under T. W. Gordon.

articles.text: The sheriff's sale of the Cantonment property took place last Monday according to advertisement. There was a good turn-out and prices were bid up in almost all cases to a high figure. The stock was sold first, the mares bringing fair figures in nearly every case. The cows and calves sold low. Harness, saddles, wagons, furniture, carpets etc., brought first rate figures and in some instances more than they could be bought for new. Four yearling colts were about the best property. They were bid in by Ferris & Merrifield for $155 and sold for $200 before they even had a chance to pay for them. E. G. Paddock obtained the choicest of the mares, he securing three good animals and the Norman stallion. The rest were bid in by M. Wadsworth, Link Gates, Jim Harmon, T. R. Selmes and Messers. Zirngebel and Scales of Belfield. As stated the horses brought fair prices but they were good animals and we doubt if there is a purchaser who is dissatisfied with his bargain.
articles.summary: Report of the sheriff's sale of the Cantonment property, with buyers including Ferris & Merrifield and E. G. Paddock.

City Drug Store, Medora, Dak. — drugs, patent medicines, perfumery, toilet articles, notions, periodicals, stationery; H. M. Jorgens, Proprietor
E. J. Owenhouse, Bozeman, Mont. — stock saddles, Concord harness, bits and spurs, chaparajos, reatas, quirts, hackamores
Minneapolis & St. Louis Ry, "Famous Albert Lea Route"
articles.summary: Classified notices and display ads on page 4.

articles.text:
Brand: E. W. Casey, Frank S. Moore, Manager, P.O. Medora, Billings Co., Dak. — KC on left hip and shoulder (F); 2nd brand same without circle; range O'Donnell creek; no cattle branded as above for sale
Brand: Sloping Bottom Ranch, Lloyd Roberts, Proprietor, P.O. Medora — brand on left hip; range Little Missouri 7 miles south of N. P. R. R.; horse brand same on left shoulder
Brand: Badger Cattle Company, Howard Eaton, M'g'r, P.O. Medora, Billings Co. — VI on left hip, horse brand same; range Beaver creek and Little Missouri river
Brand: Dorr Clark, Spearfish, Dakota — VVV on left side, also one or two V's on either side; ear mark under-bit in left ear; range Belle Fourche
Brand: Clark & Plum, Spearfish, Dakota — E6 on left side; left ear cropped; range Grand river; additional brands ZD, DZ, ZD (bar), circle cross; $100 reward re VVV or E6 ranges
Brand: Little Missouri Horse Company, E. R. Tarbell, M'n'g'r, Medora — brand on left shoulder; range Davis creek and Little Missouri river
Brand: W. N. Thompson & Co., Wm. Dantz, Manager, P.O. Medora — quarter-circle diamond and TD on left hip; tip of left ear cut off square; additional brands quarter-circle diamond on left side and T on left hip
Brand: LeMoyne Cattle Co. (Limited), D. K. Wade, Manager, Medora — LC on left side and reversed C on right hip; range Little Missouri south of the R. R.; ranch Tepee bottom; crop the right; horse brand LC on left shoulder; owners of DW brand
Brand: Soho Cattle Co., Chas. Eaton, Manager, Medora — SO on left side; swallow fork right ear and crop left; range Little Missouri river and Beaver north of N. P. R. R.
Brand: Garner Creek Horse Ranch, J. A. VanEeghen, Prop., Medora — VE low down on left hip; range Garner creek eight miles from mouth
Brand: Chimney Butte Ranch, Theodore Roosevelt, Proprietor; Ferris & Merrifield, Managers, P.O. Medora — Maltese cross on left hip, or right side, both or either; down cut dewlap; range six miles south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri
Brand: Bullion Creek Horse Ranch, Jack Bullion, Prop., Medora — SS on left hip; range Bullion creek twenty miles south of Medora
Brand: N. P. Refrigerator Car Co., Medora — Y-cross brand on left side; also owner of steers purchased of Mason & Lovell branded -H- and 7L; calf mark left ear grubbed; ranges Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: Ætna Ranch, Osborne Bros., Managers, P.O. Medora — Æ on either side; range Andrews creek N of Sentinel Butte
Brand: Berry, Boice & Co., P.O. Keith, Montana — 777 on right hip, side and shoulder; grub the right ear; horse brand same on right hip; range south of N. P. R. R. on Little Missouri river and Beaver creek
Brand: E. G. Paddock, P.O. Medora — six-inch circle-dot on both sides well up; range six miles north of crossing of N. P. R. R. and Little Missouri; horse brand four-inch circle-dot on left shoulder and left hip

Brand: Neimmela Ranch, Gregor Lang, Manager, P.O. Medora — thistle on left or right shoulder; vent bar under thistle; range Keogh crossing of Little Missouri to Pretty butte; 2nd and 3rd brands

articles.summary: Cattle and horse brand advertisements, including Theodore Roosevelt's Chimney Butte Ranch.

events.date_basis: "within the last three weeks" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Worst prairie fires since settlement sweep western Dakota and the Bad Lands
events.summary: The paper reported the most extensive prairie fires since settlement, from Jamestown to between Mingusville and Glendive and from the Yellowstone to the Cave Hills, with fire led into the Bad Lands along coulies and the air still full of smoke. It warned that winter range would be short.
events.excerpt: Never, since this country was first settled, have there been such extensive and destructive prairie fires as have raged within the last three weeks.

events.date_basis: "Monday" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: T. R. Selmes attends the Cantonment sales
events.summary: T. R. Selmes of Mandan was in town attending the Cantonment sales as attorney for the estate.
events.excerpt: T. R. Selmes of Mandan, was in town Monday attending the Cantonment sales, he being attorney for the estate.

events.date_basis: "this morning" in issue of Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Abe Goodkind of Bismarck in town selling cigars
events.summary: Abe Goodkind of Bismarck was in Medora praising the "Far West" and "Our Pet" cigars.
events.excerpt: making the buttes and coulies fairly ring with praises of the "Far West" and "Our Pet" cigars.

events.date_basis: arrived "Sunday night", left "Tuesday" (29 Sep) before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Judge Francis and clerk Haight stay with the Marquis de Morès en route to Deadwood court
events.summary: Judge Francis and Supreme Court clerk Haight arrived Sunday night and left Tuesday for the court session at Deadwood; while in Medora they were guests of the Marquis.
events.excerpt: While here they were guests of the Marquis.

events.date_basis: "yesterday" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Deer killed by train at Sully Springs
events.summary: A deer was killed by the cars at Sully Springs, the only such case the paper knew of.
events.excerpt: A deer was killed by the cars at Sully Springs yesterday

events.date_basis: "Monday" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Osborne Bros.' Polled Angus heifer killed by train
events.summary: One of Osborne Bros.' Polled Angus heifers was killed by a train; the paper expected the railroad to pay no more than for an ordinary animal.
events.excerpt: One of Osborne Bros. Polled Angus heifers was killed by a train Monday.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: A. T. Packard advertises cattle for sale
events.summary: Packard offered six cows, twelve two-year-old steers, ninety heifers, nine yearling heifers and two bulls from Minnesota and Iowa, with horses and outfit if desired.
events.excerpt: The stock is all in good condition and is from Minnesota and Iowa.

events.date_basis: "this fall", stated in issue of Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Maltese Cross, Quarter Circle Diamond and LC outfits to winter bulls near the Big Plateau
events.summary: The Maltese Cross, Quarter Circle Diamond and LC outfits planned to gather all their bulls this fall and feed them near the Big Plateau, with hay already provided.
events.excerpt: The Maltese cross, Quarter circle diamond and L C outfits will gather all their bulls this fall and feed them near the Big Plateau.

events.date_basis: "this winter", stated in issue of Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Outfits to test keeping cattle off the river bottoms this winter
events.summary: Several outfits made preparations to keep their cattle back from the river this winter to test the practice, though the fires cut the feed by at least a third.
events.excerpt: Several outfits have made preparations to keep all their cattle back from the river, and thoroughly test the matter.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Bad Lands Cattle Co. cattle sell low in Chicago; Will Dantz's shipment suffers en route
events.summary: Bad Lands Cattle Co. cattle brought only $3.85 and $4 in Chicago, being under 1,200 lbs. Will Dantz's cattle refused food and water and were kept off their feet by slippery car floors after St. Paul.
events.excerpt: the Bad Lands cattle Co's cattle, only brought $3.85 and $4.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday morning" before Thu 1 Oct 1885; remounted "yesterday" (30 Sep)
events.title: Bill Jones thrown twice by a broncho as the round-up starts
events.summary: Bill Jones was thrown twice by a bucking broncho when the round-up started, was patched up in town and rode out again the next morning.
events.excerpt: Bill Jones tackled a broncho when the round-up started, Tuesday morning, that could have given points to Mark Twain's prize bucker.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Refrigerator Car Co. moves general offices to Medora
events.summary: The general offices of the Refrigerator Car Co. were moved from St. Paul to Medora.
events.excerpt: The general offices of the Ref. Car Co. have been moved from St. Paul to Medora.

events.date_basis: "this morning" in issue of Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: 500 Hashknife cattle delivered to the Co.
events.summary: J. W. Buster superintended delivery of five hundred Hashknife cattle averaging 1,066 lbs to the Co.
events.excerpt: J. W. Buster superintended the delivery of five hundred Hashknife cattle to the Co. this morning averaging 1066.

events.date_basis: no date given; week before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: John Carr of Delavan, Ill., goes home with a better opinion of Dakota
events.summary: John Carr of Delavan, Illinois, returned home from a visit to Dick with a much improved idea of Dakota and sent the paper late papers from home.
events.excerpt: He returned home from his visit to Dick, with a very much and favorably changed idea of Dakota.

events.date_basis: "last week" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Geo. Porter leaves on annual purchasing tour for the company store
events.summary: Geo. Porter left for Chicago and the east on his annual buying trip for the company's general store; Keeler and Grymes ran the store in his absence.
events.excerpt: Geo. Porter left last week for Chicago and the east, on his annual purchasing tour for the Co's. general store.

events.date_basis: "last Saturday" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: P. S. Bemis of New York arrives and joins the round-up
events.summary: P. S. Bemis of New York, lately of Ransom county, came to Medora and joined the round-up to learn the cattle business.
events.excerpt: came to Medora last Saturday and has joined the round-up.

events.date_basis: "recent trial"; week before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Wm. Roberts convicted of stealing Hashknife horses
events.summary: At Miles City Wm. Roberts was found guilty of stealing six horses at the Hashknife camp last winter and was reportedly sentenced to sixteen years.
events.excerpt: Wm. Roberts was found guilty of stealing six horses at the Hashknife camp last winter.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday morning" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Fall round-up leaves Medora, working through heavy smoke
events.summary: The round-up started from Medora and by the issue date was at Wadsworth's; smoke from the fires troubled the riders, and missed cattle were expected to mean more mavericks in spring.
events.excerpt: The round-up started from Medora Tuesday morning and is now at Wadsworths

events.date_basis: "Saturday" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Supt. Green inspects ground for new Medora stock yards
events.summary: Supt. Green looked over the ground for new stock yards at Medora; large ones were expected because feed was scarce at Dickinson and Mingusville.
events.excerpt: Supt. Green was in town Saturday looking over the ground preparatory to building new stock yards here.

events.date_basis: "Monday" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Belfield men attend Medora sale with prize potato
events.summary: Postmaster Harbison, G. H. Zirngebel and Geo. E. Scales of Belfield attended Monday's sale; Scales brought the season's prize potato raised near Belfield.
events.excerpt: The latter chartered a flat-car or something and brought along the prize potato of the season.

events.date_basis: "last Saturday evening" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Julius LeMoyne arrives; LC herd to winter on present range
events.summary: Julius LeMoyne, president of the LeMoyne Cattle Co., arrived from Pennsylvania. The LC herd will stay on its range this winter, and he was considering a blooded herd to raise range bulls.
events.excerpt: It has been decided to keep the LC herd on its present range for this winter at least.

events.date_basis: "Tuesday and yesterday" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Joseph Nimmo Jr. visits Medora and the Cow Boy office
events.summary: Jos. W. Nimmo, Jr., former chief of the Bureau of Statistics, spent two days in Medora and called at the Cow Boy while gathering facts for a work on cattle raising; he was to go east the next morning and return to stop at Miles City.
events.excerpt: was here Tuesday and yesterday and made us a very pleasant call.

events.date_basis: "last Monday" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Sheriff's sale of the Cantonment property
events.summary: The sheriff's sale of the Cantonment property drew a good turnout. Mares brought fair prices, cows and calves sold low and harness and furniture sold high; E. G. Paddock got the best mares and the Norman stallion.
events.excerpt: The sheriff's sale of the Cantonment property took place last Monday according to advertisement.

events.date_basis: "last Monday" before Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Ferris & Merrifield buy and resell four yearling colts at the Cantonment sale
events.summary: Ferris & Merrifield, managers of Roosevelt's Chimney Butte Ranch, bid in four yearling colts for $155 and sold them for $200 before paying for them.
events.excerpt: They were bid in by Ferris & Merrifield for $155 and sold for $200 before they even had a chance to pay for them.

events.date_basis: notice in issue of Thu 1 Oct 1885; removal date not given
events.title: Chas. Cook selling out before leaving Medora
events.summary: Chas. Cook announced he would sell all goods in his store at cost for cash, along with counters and fixtures, before his removal from Medora.
events.excerpt: Previous to my removal from Medora, I will sell all goods in my store

events.date_basis: standing ad in issue of Thu 1 Oct 1885
events.title: Chimney Butte Ranch brand advertised: Theodore Roosevelt, proprietor
events.summary: The brand column carried the Chimney Butte Ranch ad naming Theodore Roosevelt as proprietor and Ferris & Merrifield as managers, with the Maltese cross brand and range six miles south of the N. P. R. R. on the Little Missouri.
events.excerpt: Chimney Butte Ranch. Theodore Roosevelt, Proprietor; Ferris & Merrifield, Managers
